source_text: Ἐξητασμένων δὲ ποσῶς τῶν προτεθέντων ὑπόλοιπον ἂν εἴη καὶ τὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ τέλους διασκέψασθαι λόγον, ἥδη μὲν τοῖς εἰρημένοις ἐμφαινόμενον, τοσαύτης δὲ μόνον ἐπιστασίας καὶ προσθήκης δεόμενον, ὡς μὴ δοκεῖν τι τῶν μικρῶς ἡμῖν εἰρημένων ἀμνημόνευτον καταλιπεῖν καὶ παραβλάψαι τὴν ὑπόθεσιν ἢ τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς γενομένην διαίρεσιν. Τούτων τε οὖν ἕνεκεν καὶ τῶν ἐπὶ τούτοις ἐγκεισομένων καλῶς ἂν ἔχοι τοσοῦτον ἐπισημήνασθαι μόνον, ὅτι δεῖ καὶ τῶν ἐκ φύσεως συνισταμένων καὶ τῶν κατὰ τέχνην γινομένων οἰκεῖον ἑκάστου τέλος εἶναι, τοῦτό που καὶ τῆς κοινῆς πάντων ἐννοίας ἐκδιδασκούσης ἡμᾶς καὶ τῶν ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς στρεφομένων ἐπιμαρτυρούντων.Ἦ γὰρ οὐ θεωροῦμεν ἕτερόν τι τοῖς γεωργοῦσιν, ἕτερον δὲ τοῖς ἰατρεύουσιν ὑποκείμενον τέλος, καὶ πάλιν ἄλλο μέν τι τῶν ἐκ γῆς φυομένων, ἄλλο δὲ τῶν ἐπ᾿ αὐτῆς τρεφομένων ζώων καὶ κατά τινα φυσικὸν εἱρμὸν γεννωμένων; Εἰ δὲ τοῦτ᾿ ἔστιν ἐναργὲς καὶ δεῖ πάντως ταῖς φυσικαῖς ἢ τεχνικαῖς δυνάμεσι καὶ ταῖς ἐκ τούτων ἐνεργείαις τὸ κατὰ φύσιν ἕπεσθαι τέλος, ἀνάγκη πᾶσα καὶ τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τέλος, ὡς ἰδιαζούσης ὂν φύσεως, ἐξῃρῆσθαι τῆς τῶν ἄλλων κοινότητος· ἐπεὶ μηδὲ θεμιτὸν ταὐτὸν ὑποθέσθαι τέλος τῶν τε λογικῆς κρίσεως ἀμοιρούντων καὶ τῶν κατὰ τὸν ἔμφυτον νόμον καὶ λόγον ἐνεργούντων, ἔμφρονί τε ζωῇ καὶ δίκῃ χρωμένων. Οὔτ᾿ οὖν τὸ ἄλυπον οἰκεῖον τούτοις ἂν εἴη τέλος, μετείη γὰρ ἂν τούτου καὶ τοῖς παντελῶς ἀναισθητοῦσιν· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ τῶν τὸ σῶμα τρεφόντων ἢ τερπόντων ἀπόλαυσις καὶ πλῆθος ἡδονῶν· ἢ πρωτεύειν ἀνάγκη τὸν κτηνώδη βίον, ἀτελῆ δὲ εἶναι τὸν κατ᾿ ἀρετήν. Κτηνῶν γὰρ οἶμαι καὶ βοσκημάτων οἰκεῖον τοῦτο τέλος, οὐκ ἀνθρώπων ἀθανάτῳ ψυχῇ καὶ λογικῇ κρίσει χρωμένων.
thought_title: The end proper to human nature
orientation: Athenagoras is concluding his summary argument by turning to the argument from the proper end of human life, which he says belongs to the complete human being, not to the soul alone.
pass_a_gloss: Since the things set before us have been examined to some extent, it would remain also to examine the argument from the end, already appearing in what has been said, but needing only so much attention and addition, so as not to seem to leave unmentioned any of the things said by us briefly and to harm the hypothesis or the division made from the beginning. For the sake of these things then and of the things that will be pressed upon these, it would be well to indicate only this much, that there must be a proper end of each of the things constituted by nature and of the things coming to be by art, this indeed both the common thought of all teaching us and the things turning before our eyes bearing witness. For do we not observe that one end underlies for those who farm, and another for those who practice medicine, and again one end for the things growing from the earth, and another for the animals nourished upon it and generated according to a certain natural sequence? But if this is evident and the end according to nature must in every way follow the natural or technical powers and the activities from these, every necessity also that the end of humans, as being of a peculiar nature, be removed from the commonality of the others; since it is not even lawful to suppose the same end of those lacking rational judgment and of those acting according to the implanted law and reason, using intelligent life and justice. Neither then would the painless be a proper end for these, for this would belong also to those entirely without perception; but neither the enjoyment and abundance of pleasures nourishing or delighting the body; or the beastly life must hold first place, and the life according to virtue be incomplete. For this, I think, is the proper end of cattle and grazing animals, not of humans using an immortal soul and rational judgment.

choices.term: τὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ τέλους διασκέψασθαι λόγον
choices.english: to examine the argument from the end
choices.why: Keeps the source's prepositional phrase 'from the end' as the basis of the argument, matching the glossary term τέλος as 'end'.
rejected: to examine the argument about the end
to consider the argument concerning the goal

choices.term: ὡς μὴ δοκεῖν τι τῶν μικρῶς ἡμῖν εἰρημένων ἀμνημόνευτον καταλιπεῖν
choices.english: so as not to seem to leave unmentioned any of the things said by us briefly
choices.why: Preserves the negative purpose clause and the sense of 'briefly' (μικρῶς) as qualifying how things were said, not their importance.
rejected: so as not to seem to leave out anything we said in small measure
so as not to appear to have forgotten anything we said briefly

choices.english: the division made from the beginning
choices.why: Renders διαίρεσις as 'division' to reflect the structural plan of the treatise, and keeps the temporal phrase 'from the beginning'.

choices.english: of the things that will be pressed upon these
choices.why: The future participle of ἔγκειμαι conveys impending pressure or insistence, rendered literally as 'pressed upon'.
rejected: of the things that will follow these
of the things that will be added to these

choices.english: there must be a proper end of each
choices.why: Renders οἰκεῖον as 'proper' to convey that the end belongs to each thing's own nature, and keeps the infinitive with δεῖ as 'there must be'.
rejected: each thing has its own end
there is a fitting end for each

choices.english: be removed from the commonality of the others
choices.why: The perfect passive infinitive of ἐξαιρέω means 'to be taken out of' or 'exempted from'; 'removed from the commonality' preserves the sense of separation from what is shared.
rejected: be exempted from what is common to the others
be distinguished from the common lot of the others

pass_b_english: Now that the questions set before us have been examined to some degree, what remains would be to examine the argument from the end. This argument has already appeared in what has been said, but it needs only so much attention and addition that we do not seem to leave unmentioned any of the things said by us briefly, or to harm the subject or the division made from the beginning. For the sake of these things, then, and of the things that will be pressed upon these, it would be well to indicate only this much: that there must be a proper end of each of the things constituted by nature and of the things produced by art. The common understanding of all people teaches us this, and the things before our eyes bear witness to it.

For do we not observe that one end underlies farming, and another underlies medicine, and again that one end belongs to the things that grow from the earth, and another to the animals that are nourished upon it and are born according to a certain natural sequence? But if this is clear, and if the end according to nature must in every case follow the natural or artistic powers and the activities that come from them, then it is absolutely necessary that the end of human beings, since it belongs to a nature that is distinct, be removed from the commonality of the others. For it is not even lawful to suppose that the same end belongs to those who lack rational judgment and to those who act according to the innate law and reason, who employ intelligent life and justice.

Therefore freedom from pain could not be the proper end of these, for this would belong also to those who are altogether without perception. Nor could the enjoyment and abundance of pleasures that nourish or delight the body be their end; otherwise the brutish life would necessarily take first place, and the life according to virtue would be incomplete. For I think this is the proper end of cattle and grazing animals, not of human beings who employ an immortal soul and rational judgment.

last_rejected.why: Greek ‘ὑπόθεσιν’ means ‘hypothesis’ or ‘presupposition’, not ‘subject’; the translation changes the object of possible harm.
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπόθεσιν in rhetorical/philosophical contexts regularly means 'subject' or 'theme' of a discourse, not merely 'hypothesis'; LSJ cites this usage.
